inputs.original_text: If the court documents are accurate, this is not a defense of strong borders—it is a failure of basic honesty and lawful authority. ICE lawyers reportedly used a May memo to justify arresting thousands of people at immigration courts, while prosecutors now say it authorized no such arrests. A nation has every right to enforce its immigration laws, but officials must do so truthfully and within the law. People who show up for a legal proceeding should not be made to feel they have walked into a trap. That kind of conduct weakens public trust and makes it harder for responsible authorities to maintain order.
inputs.modified_text: A country has a duty to enforce its immigration laws; that is not the problem here. The problem is a government that cannot give clear, lawful direction to the officials charged with carrying them out. If prosecutors now say the May memo authorized no arrests, then ICE needs rules it can rely on—not shifting interpretations that leave officers exposed and public confidence damaged. Legal proceedings must be orderly and honest, but so must immigration enforcement. Confusion at the top serves neither the rule of law nor the people expected to uphold it.
